hero.name: Tanvi
hero.who: a 24-year-old pharmacy assistant in Guwahati who draws every night but shows nobody

story.b: From nine to six, Tanvi stands behind the counter of a small pharmacy in Guwahati, reading prescriptions and counting strips of tablets. At night, in her room, she draws. Tiny ink drawings of the city: the ferry crossing the Brahmaputra, a momo stall in the rain, old Assam-type houses with tin roofs. She has filled eleven sketchbooks. Her art account has four posts, the last one two years old. She tells herself she will share when she is good enough. Then her cousin in Bengaluru asks her to draw a wedding invitation. At the wedding, a guest holds the card and asks where she can see more of this artist's work. There is nowhere to see more. Tanvi smiles politely, and feels the sting all the way home.

ask.q: Tanvi wants people to find her work but feels she is not good enough yet. What should she do first?
o: Wait until she has finished a proper art course
Pay for ads to push her drawings to strangers
Start sharing small, honest pieces now, as someone still learning
ask.why: Waiting for a course or for perfect skill can stretch on for years, and nobody can find work kept in a drawer. Ads push people toward work they have no reason to care about yet. Sharing honestly as a learner lets people discover her and grow with her.

chapters.take: You do not need to be an expert to start sharing.

story.b: Tanvi decides to share like a learner, not an expert. Every Sunday she posts one drawing and a short note on what she struggled with that week. Her first note is about hands. She cannot draw them, so she posts a page of terrible ones next to a slightly better rickshaw puller gripping his handlebar. She expects silence. Instead, two art students from Cotton University comment that hands defeat them too. One shares a trick with simple boxes. Another invites her to a Sunday morning sketch meet at the riverfront. Tanvi goes, nervous, with her pencil case. Eight people sit on the steps drawing boats and chatting. Nobody there is an expert. Everyone is learning, and somehow that makes her want to draw more.

ask.q: Tanvi's new drawing has awkward, clumsy hands. Should she post it?
o: Yes, with a note on what she is struggling with and trying next
No, she should post only her best, most finished pieces
Yes, but crop out the hands so nobody notices
ask.why: People connect with a learner who is honest about the hard parts, and her note invites others who struggle with the same thing. Posting only polished work hides the growth people enjoy watching. Cropping the mistake keeps the fear and loses the lesson.

chapters.take: Share what you are learning, not just what you have mastered.

story.b: Tanvi notices that people linger longer on her rough sketches than on finished ones. So she starts showing the steps. A pencil outline made on the city bus. The ink version during her lunch break behind the pharmacy shelves. A short clip of her laying blue wash over the river, with a line on why she kept the sky pale. A regular customer at the pharmacy recognises her from the clip and asks about the ferry drawing. A week later, the owner of a small cafe in Pan Bazaar messages her. He wants a painted menu wall and asks what her process would look like. Tanvi sends him her rough thumbnails, three colour options and her reasons for each. He replies within an hour.

ask.q: The cafe owner asks Tanvi for samples before hiring her. What would build the most trust?
o: Send only three finished, polished pieces
Show a finished piece with her rough sketches and why she made each choice
Offer to paint the wall for free so he takes no risk
ask.why: Finished pieces show what she can do, but the rough steps show how she thinks and works, which is what a client is really trusting. Working for free undervalues her and still says nothing about her process. Letting him see the making builds real confidence.

chapters.take: Showing how you make something builds more trust than the result alone.

story.b: Tanvi has a grand idea: stay quiet for months, then launch a full Guwahati series of thirty drawings at once. Her friend from the sketch meet gently points out that big launches often land in silence. So Tanvi changes the plan. Every night after dinner she spends fifteen minutes sharing one small thing, a sketch, a colour test, a note about a building she loves. She also builds a simple free website that holds all her work in one place, with a small sign-up box for updates. When one app suddenly shows her posts to fewer people, she panics for a day. Then she notices her website still gets visitors, many from the QR code printed on the cafe menu.

ask.q: Tanvi's friend plans to stay silent for six months, then launch a big collection. What would serve her better?
o: Stick to the big launch, since one big splash gets the most attention
Post only when she feels inspired, so quality stays high
Share a small piece regularly and keep a simple page of her own
ask.why: A single launch after months of silence often lands with nobody watching, and posting only when inspired usually means posting rarely. A steady trickle gives people a reason to come back, and a page she owns keeps her work findable even if one app changes.

chapters.take: Show up a little, often, in a place that belongs to you.

story.b: A follower asks how Tanvi gets the soft rain effect in her street scenes. Her first instinct is to keep it secret, in case others copy her. Then she remembers how the boxes trick for hands helped her. She records a short video showing exactly how she does it, step by step, and the post becomes her most shared one. People who try it tag her, and new followers arrive through them. She also starts a small series about what inspires her. Her favourite is about Dilip da, an old signboard painter near Fancy Bazaar whose hand-lettered shop names she has studied for years. She photographs his boards, names him, and explains what she learned. He asks his grandson to show him the post, twice.

ask.q: Tanvi learned her lettering style by watching an old signboard painter. When she posts new lettering, what should she do?
o: Name the painter and share what she learned from him
Keep quiet about it so her style looks original
Mention him only if someone accuses her of copying
ask.why: Giving clear credit is honest, and showing where good ideas come from makes her more trustworthy, not less. Hiding her influence risks looking dishonest later, and waiting for an accusation turns generosity into defence. Credit costs nothing and builds goodwill.

chapters.take: Teach what you know and credit who taught you. People trust you more.

story.b: In the monsoon, everything slows down. Fewer likes, fewer comments, and one stranger writes that her work looks childish. Tanvi reads it at the pharmacy counter between customers and feels her face burn. That night she types a sharp reply, then deletes it. She looks at the comment again. It has nothing specific in it, nothing she can use. A week earlier, though, a retired art teacher had kindly pointed out that her buildings lean because her lines do not meet properly. That one she can use. She spends the quiet month practising perspective on the sketch meet steps. She also leaves warm, specific comments for three other young artists she admires. She keeps posting every night, even when almost nobody responds.

ask.q: During a quiet month, a stranger calls Tanvi's work childish. What should she do?
o: Reply with a sharp comeback so others see she is confident
Ignore the vague insult, use any useful feedback, and keep posting
Take a break from posting until the comments improve
ask.why: Vague insults offer nothing to learn from, and arguing only feeds them. Stopping hands the critic a win and loses momentum just when steadiness matters most. Separating real feedback from noise, and simply continuing, is how creators survive slow stretches and find their people.

chapters.take: Learn from useful criticism, ignore the noise, and keep going.

story.b: By winter, Tanvi's painted wall covers one side of the cafe in Pan Bazaar: the ferry, the momo stall, the tin roofs, and a small signboard in Dilip da's style. People photograph it with their coffee. She still works at the pharmacy, still counts strips of tablets, still draws every night. The difference is that people can now find her. Her website has a few hundred people signed up for updates. Two wedding card orders came through her cousin's friends. The Sunday sketch meet has grown to twenty, and Tanvi now brings spare pencils for newcomers. Her eleven sketchbooks are still under the bed, but the twelfth sits open on her desk, half of it already shared.

chapters.take: Sharing honestly, a little at a time, lets the right people find you.
